original_idea: Acho que pessoas que cozinham para uma ou duas pessoas desperdiçam menos alimentos se receberem sugestões de refeições baseadas no que já têm em casa e no prazo de validade aproximado. Gostaria de testar se isso realmente muda o comportamento delas.
current_idea: Test whether providing personalized meal suggestions based on users' manually entered pantry items and their approximate expiration dates reduces food waste among individuals cooking for one or two people.
human_intent: To test whether giving such tailored meal suggestions changes users' behavior and reduces food waste.
problem_statement: People cooking for one or two persons may waste food because they lack meal suggestions that utilize the ingredients they already have and consider the approximate expiration dates of those ingredients.
actors_or_users: Individuals cooking for one or two people
assumptions: Users know what ingredients they have and their expiration dates
Users are willing to follow suggested meals
The system can access or be provided with pantry data
Food waste can be measured accurately
Suggestions can be generated based on available data
ambiguities: How the pantry inventory will be collected
How behavior change will be measured
Whether suggestions are delivered via app, website, or other means
User privacy concerns regarding pantry data
strengths: Targets a specific user segment (small households)

critical_issues.issue: Reliance on user‑provided pantry data that may be incomplete or inaccurate
critical_issues.why_it_matters: Incorrect ingredient lists can lead to unsuitable meal suggestions, causing increased waste or even health risks
Self‑reported waste is prone to bias, making it impossible to validate the core hypothesis of waste reduction

critical_issues.issue: User willingness to follow suggested meals is uncertain
critical_issues.why_it_matters: If users ignore suggestions due to taste, time, or habit, the system cannot achieve its intended impact

critical_issues.issue: Privacy concerns around sharing pantry inventories
critical_issues.why_it_matters: Reluctance to provide detailed ingredient data may limit data availability, undermining the system’s functionality

fragile_assumptions: Users know what ingredients they have and their expiration dates
Users are willing to follow suggested meals
The system can access or be provided with pantry data
Food waste can be measured accurately
Suggestions can be generated based on available data
contradictions: Assuming users know expiration dates contradicts common consumer behavior where dates are often forgotten
Assuming the system can freely access pantry data conflicts with typical privacy expectations
Assuming suggestions alone will change cooking habits ignores other motivational factors
failure_modes: Inaccurate pantry input leads to irrelevant or unsafe meal suggestions
Users disengage due to suggestion fatigue or lack of taste alignment
Measurement errors produce misleading conclusions about waste reduction
Data privacy restrictions prevent sufficient data collection

alternatives.mechanism: Implement a smartphone‑based image capture system that uses AI to recognize pantry items and estimate expiration dates from photos taken by the user
addresses_issues: Reliance on user‑provided pantry data that may be incomplete or inaccurate
Privacy concerns around sharing pantry inventories
tradeoffs: Requires users to take photos regularly, increasing effort
AI recognition may misidentify items or miss small packages
Images are stored or processed, raising additional privacy considerations
alternatives.novelty_or_difference: Uses visual AI instead of manual entry to build a more accurate inventory

alternatives.mechanism: Partner with grocery store loyalty programs and smart‑container IoT devices to automatically import purchase data and monitor weight/temperature changes that infer consumption and expiration
addresses_issues: Reliance on user‑provided pantry data that may be incomplete or inaccurate
Privacy concerns around sharing pantry inventories
tradeoffs: Requires commercial partnerships and user consent for data sharing
IoT hardware adds cost and may have adoption barriers
Potential technical failures in weight/temperature sensing could produce inaccurate data
alternatives.novelty_or_difference: Combines purchase‑history integration with sensor‑based tracking for passive, continuous inventory updates

alternatives.mechanism: Introduce a gamified suggestion platform that offers points, badges, or discounts for following meal plans and for users to log leftover quantities via quick taps, using statistical models to estimate overall waste reduction
addresses_issues: User willingness to follow suggested meals is uncertain
Privacy concerns around sharing pantry inventories
tradeoffs: Self‑reported data can be biased or incomplete
Gamification may attract users primarily for rewards rather than genuine behavior change
Incentive costs need to be covered by sponsors or ads
alternatives.novelty_or_difference: Leverages behavioral incentives and lightweight self‑reporting to improve adherence and estimate waste without deep inventory data

core_mechanism: A web/mobile app that lets users manually input the items they have at home and their estimated expiration dates, then generates personalized meal suggestions that use those items before they spoil.
core_mechanism_justification: This mechanism directly follows the user's expressed desire for a low‑effort solution that relies on user‑provided data, avoiding complex hardware or AI image processing while still enabling targeted suggestions to reduce waste.

known_risks: Low user engagement may limit data quality
Inaccurate manual entry could lead to suboptimal suggestions
Potential bias in self‑reported waste data
recommended_next_step: Build a minimal viable product of the manual‑entry suggestion app, recruit a small pilot group of 20‑30 individuals cooking for one or two people, collect baseline waste data, run the intervention for 4 weeks, and evaluate changes in reported food waste.
tested_core_mechanism: A web/mobile app that lets users manually input the items they have at home and their estimated expiration dates, then generates personalized meal suggestions that use those items before they spoil.
reality_dependencies: Consistent user input of pantry items and expiration dates
Accurate mapping of entered items to recipes that use them before spoilage
Access to a comprehensive recipe database with ingredient quantities
Ability to track food waste (e.g., self‑reported waste logs) for measurement
Internet connectivity for data sync and app updates
claims_needing_evidence: Personalized meal suggestions reduce household food waste for 1‑2 person households
Users will regularly update pantry inventory with accurate expiration dates
Suggested meals are acceptable and will be prepared by users
Waste reduction can be reliably measured through self‑reported data
candidate_tests: Conduct a 4‑week randomized controlled trial where one group uses the app and a control group does not; measure food waste via weekly waste logs

Run an algorithm validation study comparing suggested meals to actual pantry contents to ensure ingredient match before expiry
Survey participants after app use to evaluate satisfaction with meal suggestions and perceived waste reduction
exploratory_candidate_tests: Prototype AI‑based image capture to auto‑populate pantry items and compare entry time versus manual entry
Pilot integration with a grocery loyalty program to auto‑import purchase data and assess impact on inventory accuracy
Implement a gamified points system and test its effect on user engagement and frequency of waste reporting
